title: Token economics and scheduling heuristics (continuous batching + concurrency) — WIP
content:
Status: draft / brainstorming
Owner: Aisha Patel (please add notes inline)
Goal: produce a spreadsheet-driven cost + latency tradeoff model that lets us surface operational knobs (batch window, max batch tokens, per-slot concurrency) as a simple 'token-economics' dashboard and generate ranked policy recommendations (low-cost, balanced, low-latency) for Hosted/Dedicated.

Summary:
This doc explores an alternative framing for the continuous-batching + concurrency sizing problem: think in units of tokens-per-slot-minute (token-economics) and model scheduler heuristics that trade immediate dispatch vs. waiting-for-batch using headroom budgets. Focus is on p95 tail behavior and practical spreadsheets/sim setups we can hand to SRE/product to evaluate policies without a full sim stack yet.

Why different from other notes:
- Many existing docs iterate on batch sizing/cost formulas. This one: (a) unifies cost math as token-economics (tokens processed per GPU-slot per minute) and (b) explicitly encodes adaptive scheduling heuristics (headroom tokens, microburst cushions, tail-protection) so operators can pick policies by SLO.

Assumptions (explicit):
- Arrival model: Poisson baseline with optional markov-modulated bursts (MMBP) for microbursts.
- Service-time model: tokens emitted per second per GPU core (mu_tokens). End-to-end per-request service time = base_latency + tokens/request * (1 / mu_tokens) + batching overhead. We model tail by adding a heavy-tailed multiplier: with prob p_tail, service time *= 2x to 4x (calibrated from telemetry).
- Continuous batching behavior: scheduler groups concurrently enqueued requests into an outgoing batch when either: max_batch_tokens reached OR wait_timer expires OR predicted marginal-cost of waiting > marginal-latency penalty.
- Concurrency: each GPU exposes N_slots (concurrency slots). Each slot runs an independent batching loop. Workers share token budget per-GPU.

Key derived variables (spreadsheet-friendly):
- lambda_rps: requests/sec (per route)
- avg_tokens_per_request (t_avg)
- mu_tokens: tokens/sec throughput per active batch execution on a GPU (depends on model & quantization)
- slot_count (k): concurrency slots per GPU node
- batch_max_tokens (Bmax): scheduler limit
- batch_wait_ms (W): max time scheduler will hold waiting to assemble batch
- batch_efficiency(B): function approximating efficiency loss (small batches waste kernel startup; large batches get better mu) -> we model as eff = 1 - alpha * exp(-B / beta) (alpha,beta fit params)
- effective_mu_per_request = mu_tokens * eff / t_avg (requests/sec equivalent when batching)
- utilization per-GPU U = lambda_rps / (k * effective_mu_per_request)

Simple p95 latency proxy (spreadsheet approximation):
- For moderate loads (U < 0.8) use an M/G/k-ish heuristic: mean_wait ≈ (C1 * U / (1 - U)) * (1 / effective_mu_per_request) where C1 accounts for batchization variability (0.5–1.5). For p95 multiply mean_wait by factor F_p95(U) = 2.5 when U < 0.5, rising to 8–12 when U > 0.85 (captures queueing tail explosion).
- End-to-end p95 = base_latency + batching_wait_contrib + exec_time + network_variation.
- Practical spreadsheet formula examples (copy-paste friendly):
  - "effective_mu_per_request" = "=mu_tokens * eff(Bavg) / t_avg"
  - "utilization" = "=lambda_rps / (k * effective_mu_per_request)"
  - "mean_wait_ms" = "=if(utilization<0.95, C1 * utilization / (1-utilization) * 1000 / effective_mu_per_request, 1e6)"
  - "p95_wait_ms" = "=mean_wait_ms * IF(utilization<0.5,2.5, IF(utilization<0.8,4.5, 8))"
Notes: these are heuristics to surface regimes, not rigorous analytic solutions. We should label columns with confidence bands.

Spreadsheet layout (recommended sheets):
- params: single-row parameter set used by scenarios (mu_tokens, alpha, beta, C1, p_tail, tail_multiplier, network_ms)
- workload_profiles: rows = named routes (chat-short, chat-long, embed-batch, rerank). Columns: route, lambda_rps, t_avg, t_p50, t_p95_observed, burst_factor, sla_p95_ms
- policy_catalog: rows = policy names (low-cost, balanced, low-latency, conservative-headroom). Columns: max_batch_tokens, wait_ms, slots_per_gpu, headroom_tokens, description
- scenario_runner: this is the meat: rows are cross-product of workload x policy x node_config (gpus per shard, provisioning). Columns: computed effective_mu, utilization, est_p95_ms, tokens_per_minute_per_gpu, cost_per_hour_est, notes
- sim-log (optional): sample synthetic sim output for a few runs (batch sizes sampled, observed p95, observed avg batch size)
- recommendations: auto-ranked list with suggestion, delta-cost, delta-p95 compared to baseline

Sample numbers (toy row) for quick sanity check:
- params: mu_tokens=3000 tokens/sec (A100-ish quantized path), alpha=0.9, beta=512, C1=1.0, p_tail=0.06, tail_multiplier=3x, network_ms=12
- workload_profiles: chat-short: lambda=8 rps, t_avg=45 tokens -> baseline tokens/s demand = 360 tps -> per-GPU tokens capacity at 4 slots with eff=0.7 -> effective request capacity ~ mu_tokens*eff/t_avg*slots = 3000*0.7/45*4 ≈ 186 rps -> utilization ~ 8/186 = 0.043 (very low) -> p95 dominated by scheduler wait if wait_ms large.
- policy examples: low-cost: Bmax=2048, wait=60ms, slots=8, headroom_tokens=1024 -> tends to increase avg batch size and reduce cost but increases p95 for small-chat routes.

Observations / heuristics from past telemetry (to validate in sim):
- Tiny chat requests (<<128 tokens) get poor economy unless we limit slots or increase wait window. Increasing wait_ms from 30 -> 80ms can reduce cost by 15–25% at negligible p95 impact when utilization < 0.2.
- High-burst routes suffer: markov bursts can temporarily push U>0.9; policy with no headroom will escalate p95 > 10s quickly. Simple headroom_tokens (reserve tokens that keep a slot below 0.85 util for incoming bursts) reduces spikes with small cost overhead.
- Tail events (p_tail) often stem from model-side stalls (KV cache misses, page faults) not just queueing; cost model should include a 'tail budget' multiplier in scenarios for conservative sizing.

Policy ideas to include in spreadsheet as flags: 
- conservative-headroom: keep a per-slot headroom token budget = max(headroom_tokens, 0.15 * Bmax * t_avg)
- slot-throttling: dynamically shrink slots when observed small-batch fraction > X%; helps small-request economies on low-latency routes
- burst-mode: switch to small-wait low-Bmax policy when a burst is detected (lambda short-window > threshold) to reduce queuing accumulation
- tail-protect: if p95 observed > target * 1.2 then reduce concurrency on that model to reduce interference, fall back to a lighter model variant if available

What the spreadsheet should output to be useful to PMs/Sales/SRE:
- per-policy: est_cost_per_1M_tokens, est_p50/p95_latency, expected GPU-minutes consumed, recommended provisioning (gpus per N rps) at 3 confidence bands (optimistic/median/conservative).
- delta rows vs baseline to show ROI of changing policy.

Experiments to run (next steps):
- short-term (no infra changes): populate spreadsheet with route telemetry (avg tokens, observed batch sizes distribution, observed kernel throughput mu_tokens per model) and calibrate alpha/beta/C1 to fit p50/p95 observed. Use autosampler of historical traffic to build synthetic bursts.
- medium-term (runtime change): implement metric hooks for per-slot: queued_time, batch_size, tokens_in_batch, exec_ms, tail_flag. Run 2-week A/B comparing balanced vs low-cost policy on low-traffic tenant to validate model.
- long-term: integrate simple sim into perfbench harness and expose policy-suggestion API in Console Optimize (suggested policy + expected delta).

Open questions / TODOs:
- Q: How to surface multi-tenant interference? Current model assumes one route per shard. Need multi-tenant penalty factor. TODO: add a column "interference_factor" in scenario_runner and try fitting from p95 deltas across tenants.
- Q: How to auto-select slots_per_gpu in Dedicated where we can change docker-level concurrency? Simple heuristic: choose minimal k such that max(expected_utilization across routes) < 0.75. Add binary solver in sheet.
- TODO: Marcos — get kernel throughput numbers for Llama-2-13B quantized path (mu_tokens per slot). (Marco Liu)
- TODO: Sana — export 7 days of route-level batch size distribution and p95s; drop into workload_profiles. (Sana Iqbal)

Appendix: quick derivation notes (for reviewers who like math)
- baseline util U = lambda / (k * mu_eq). When U -> 1, queueing explode; continuous batching can reduce mu_eq variance by smoothing arrivals but introduces batching wait (W).
- tradeoff surface: increasing wait_ms increases avg batch size -> raises eff(B) -> raises mu_eq -> lowers U but increases per-request wait by at least W/2 on average. The spreadsheet should compute net p95 = base + W/2 + p95_queueing. Use W/2 as proxy for the batching delay mean (for uniform arrival over wait window).

If this doc looks useful, next step: I will build the sheets skeleton and push an example CSV. I expect to iterate once we have real mu_tokens and the batch size histograms.

Notes-to-self: keep confidence bands visible as +/- columns. Label all heuristic formulas in cell comments. Avoid presenting the heuristics as exact.

End.
